Why America’s Military Still Needs Its Allies
item.description:
“We never fight alone. We've never done that. You can go all the way back to the days of Revolutionary War. The United States has never gone into conflict on its own. We've always built coalitions. We've always involved partners and allies. And we'll continue to do so going forward.”

That was Gen. Ronald P. Clark, Commanding General, U.S. Army Pacific Command, speaking last Tuesday at a contemporary military forum, Decisive Landpower -- Deterrence and Partner Integration Against the Pacing Threat, as part of the 2026 Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Conference in Washington, D.C.

On the panel with Clark was Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, Commander, United Nations Command, U.S. Forces Korea, and Tara Murphy Dougherty, Chief Executive Officer of Air, a leading AI software firm that specializes in national security readiness.

The two Army generals spent a good deal of their time talking about lessons learned from Ukraine and the benefits to the U.S. of allies – specifically in the Pacific. That struck me as something to further explore, since one day later, on Wednesday, President Trump continued his running criticism of allies with an October 14, Truth Social screed.

Trump said in part: “Because of the fact that we have had such Military Success, we no longer ‘need,’ or desire, the NATO Countries’ assistance — WE NEVER DID! Likewise, Japan, Australia, or South Korea. In fact, speaking as President of the United States of America, by far the Most Powerful Country Anywhere in the World, WE DO NOT NEED THE HELP OF ANYONE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

On the other hand, Gen. Brunson had told the AUSA audience one day earlier, “Everything that we do is intricately woven around the ROK (Republic of Korea)-U.S. alliance. That alliance has stood for some 75 years and it is an example or a paragon, if you will, of all that's right when folk work in alliance together. The problems that we solve are joint problems. They're not just U.S. problems. They're not just Republic of Korea problems. What they are is great opportunities for two nations to work in concert with one another in order to arrive at solutions that are beneficial for both countries.”

Gen. Clark explained further, “So our ability to be able to work with partners and allies on their sovereign soil, to be able to share procedures that we build through [military] exercises over the course of a year, some joint, some army-to-army, but always integrated with our partners. It gives us the opportunity to have our systems work technically, to have our procedures nested, and to get to know one another in a way that allows us to build the trust that's necessary in training. Because if we wait until crisis or conflict, it's too late to ask the question, can I trust

you? But because we've been working together, because we've exercised at scale, because we're modernizing our forces alongside one another, it works.”

Clark added, “We've really worked hard at building those relationships at scale inside of the land forces. We have a land forces dialogue that meets multiple times a year -- chiefs of army of Australia, Japan, the Philippines, and the U.S. We've invited the ROKs in, we've invited India in, and it continues to grow. So those relationships built army-to-army are what allows us to really integrate across interoperability, and integrate it really across our formations and with our partners in all.”

Brunson described how he and Korean Gen. Kim Sung-min, Deputy Commander of the U.S.-ROK Combined Forces Command, discussed training differently “taking advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight.”

Brunson said, “We talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion…Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the [Korean] Peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say you can't utilize the things that you've learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learned the same lessons and we've distributed ourselves in such a way that we don't make ourselves the target. We won't be moored in place.”

Clark talked about Russia, North Korea and China “learning from watching us partner, but the partnerships that our adversaries have built are transactional versus the transformational relationships that we build as a security partner of choice globally…for us it's really transformational relationships that we look to cultivate with partners and allies over time.”

Brunson described how the North Koreans, fighting for the Russians in Ukraine were “able to test systems there…and then bring that back home. So, in one aspect, they've shortened their RDT&E cycle.” He also pointed out, “The fact that you have a combat trained force with recent

combat on the [Korean] Peninsula for the first time since 1953..[and] are now bringing those lessons learned back into their own training cycle, it's shortened their time to develop them.”

Clark said that U.S. forces had also learned from Ukraine about the need for mobility and camouflage, which he described as “age-old army forgotten sciences of how to hide in plain sight and how to camouflage ourselves from observation...Our ability to be able to use electronic warfare, to be able to use just good, old-fashioned camouflage and the ability to deceive our adversary is a must. In those two theaters [Ukraine and Iran] it's not a near-peer adversary that we would be working against -- whereas, in our theater [the Pacific] it absolutely is.”

For Clark, the questions were: “How do we fight, you know, Type One, Type Two UAS [unmanned aerial system, drones]; how do we think through ballistic missile defense holistically in the region. We spend a lot of time working again with the joint force for solutions associated with that. How do we maneuver?”

Brunson raised a new issue by pointing out that, “Our old system was something [a weapons system] breaks, we send it all the way back CONUS [Continental U.S.] in order to fix it so we can then bring it all the way back out again.” That used to take 29 days by ship.

However, he added, “In the ally that we have in Korea we have a an absolutely premier industrial base, if you look at the Korea defense industry, some of the kit that we're producing right now sits along our friends, allies and partners.” Brunson said, “The Army’s new infantry squad vehicle (ISV), for example, is produced by GM Defense and GM Defense is also in the Republic of Korea.”

“So the idea of a regional sustainment hub would simply be…to bring those means of production to the theater,” Brunson suggested, noting, “In the maritime domain, when we look at maintenance, repair, and overhaul, which is being done forward alongside the Koreans, you know that 15 percent of global ship building is done in Korea. And, oh by the way, we've got an ally with a mutual defense treaty in Japan that has 10% of global ship building. And if we take these cases forward, we're able to stay in theater longer.”

The answer, Brunson said, “We've got to try to achieve admirable endurance in theater by partnering alongside our allies, seeing the things that they can do better than we can right now at distance and then keeping them right where they belong. That keeps our [military] forces forward.”

Dougherty chipped in saying: “Tens of millions of dollars saved by simply identifying things like unfilled requisitions or parts that are obsolete that can be replaced with something not obsolete and also less expensive. I think that this is it. This is part of how you generate lethality. You get readiness to pay for itself, because otherwise sustainment is too expensive when it has to be done for the entirety of the joint force all the way on the other side of the world.”

At one point, Clark said, “The secret sauce for us as an Army is our Non-Commissioned Officer (NCO) corps, reflecting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s September 30 speech praising the same group.

Clark noted that both he and Brunson were sons of NCOs, and that “with the assistance of our senior non-commissioned officers, senior enlisted leaders across the [PACOM] region have embarked upon conducting assessments with our partners and developing strategies to help them build their NCO development programs inside of their formations.”

To illustrate his point, Clark said his units had just finished an assessment in Cambodia of its army and the Commander, Gen. Mao Sophan, “basically said, ‘Hey, whatever you're asking us to do, we're going to do it because we want to get to a level of proficiency with our Non-Commissioned Officer core that we see in yours.’"

I must point out that during the one-hour-and-thirty-minute session neither General -- Clark nor Brunson -- came near to mentioning President Trump’s repeated critical views about U.S. allies.

The closest anyone came was Dougherty, who at one point said diplomatically, “We'll head into midterm elections here [in the U.S.] in November, obviously as you know, and I think we expect some variation in the political dynamic in the United States, and our allies and partners all navigate their own political changes as well.”

She then added, “If you look over the course of history, however, at least modern history, certainly the United States has invested in those partnerships. And today, we still are -- maybe with a different flavor or a different attitude. And that's not really for me to say. I'm simply observing. But we haven't lost sight of the importance of allies and partners to securing U.S. national interests.”

I would bet Clark and Brunson – along with most U.S. military professionals – would silently agree with her statement.

item.description:
DUBAI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, not seen in public since succeeding his slain father in March, a day after holding talks with representatives of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

State media said Khamenei had stressed the importance of pursuing Iran's interests and maintaining its conditions for ending the war.

item.title: Iranian strait authority says Sinokor vessels will face legal action
item.description:
DUBAI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a body set up by Tehran to manage passage requests in the Strait of Hormuz, said on Tuesday all vessels belonging to South Korean shipping company Sinokor would face "legal action" starting on November 1.

Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the strategic waterway by attacking shipping there since ​US and Israeli ⁠airstrikes on Iran on February 28. It has restricted transit to try to gain leverage over Washington, while disrupting oil flows from Arab Gulf oil producers, especially to their customers in Asia.

item.title: Three Arab states back Greece in dispute over Turkey-Libya maritime accord
item.description:
ATHENS, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Egypt, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates aligned with Greece to denounce a Turkey-Libya maritime accord as a threat to regional security and international legal order in a long-standing dispute over sea borders in the eastern Mediterranean Sea.

Libya's eastern parliamentlast week approved a maritime boundaries deal with Turkey, originally agreed in 2019, drawing swift condemnation from Greece and Cyprus, which say it infringes on their own maritime claims.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis say they launched an attack on Saudi Ras Tanura oil refinery
item.description:
DUBAI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had launched an attack on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, located on the Gulf west of the Strait of Hormuz.

The group's military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the ballistic missile attack caused a fire at the site. The Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attack.

The Houthi militia have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia since September, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.

item.title: Jordan says it killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on Syria
item.description:
Oct 27 (Reuters) - Jordan said on Tuesday it had killed more than 20 Islamic State militants in airstrikes on southern Syria the previous evening, launched in response to a deadly church attack in Jordan that authorities linked to militants operating across the border.

Syria said the strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman. Jordan regretted the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed al-Momani said in a post on X.

item.title: Two men charged in UK with helping Iran over RAF Fairford incident
item.description:
LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Two men were charged under the National Security Act on Tuesday over last month's incident at the RAF Fairford military base, with prosecutors accusing a British national of trying to help Iranian intelligence in Britain.

RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five British men were arrested outside the base in southwest England in the early hours of September 27.

item.title: China to send envoy to Middle East in near future amid conflict spillover
item.description:
BEIJING, Oct 27 (Reuters) - China is highly concerned about conflicts in the Middle East and surrounding regions and Beijing will send an envoy to the relevant countries in the near future,foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakunsaid at a daily press conference on Tuesday.

Guo called on related parties to resolve differences through dialogue and negotiation and also expressed concerns about the spillover and transmitting of the Middle East conflict to the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea region.

item.title: Alexander Solzhenitsyn warned against a war between Russians and Ukrainians. He also wanted to redraw Ukraine’s borders.
item.description: On October 20, a monument to Alexander Solzhenitsyn was dismantled in central Vladivostok, where it had stood since 2015. It was supposed to be moved to a park commemorating victims of political repression, but the very next day it was unexpectedly put back. The official explanation was that it was too large for the new site. Vladivostok’s role in this story is no coincidence. It was there that Solzhenitsyn began his journey across Russia in 1994, after 20 years in exile. The writer traveled across the country to Moscow by train. After returning, he became active in politics, criticizing Gorbachev and Yeltsin but speaking favorably of Putin. The feeling is mutual: Putin honors Solzhenitsyn’s memory despite the writer’s views on the USSR and its suppression of dissent. At Meduza’s request, historian Alexey Uvarov explains how Solzhenitsyn’s contradictory views took shape — and how they foreshadowed the Russian-Ukrainian war.

item.title: Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited
item.description:
Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited Expert comment thilton.drupal 27 October 2026

Russia’s footprint in Africa has expanded in recent years, but engagement beyond security remains uneven. The summit alone is unlikely to change this.

The third Russia–Africa Summit, which was initially announced to take place in Libya, will now take place in Moscow on 28–29 October. The summit is being portrayed as a test of Russia’s growing influence across Africa. 

Once again, considerable emphasis is being placed on how many African leaders will be attending the gathering. The Kremlin says 22 African heads of state are attending, a slight increase on the 17 that attended the summit’s second edition in St Petersburg in 2023. That marked a significant decrease from the 43 leaders that were present at the inaugural summit in Sochi in 2019. Then, the Kremlin attributed the lower turnout to ‘outrageous’ Western pressure. 

Attendance at the summit, however, is a poor measure of durable partnerships. This is particularly the case as the constraints of Russia’s partnership have become harder for African governments to overlook. 

While Russian engagement with Africa has expanded in recent years, its economic delivery remains limited and the outcomes of its security role in the Sahel have been uneven. The summit may therefore lead to new agreements, but with the war in Ukraine still constraining Russia’s resources, it is unlikely to change these fundamental dynamics. 

Summit priorities

Russia’s interest in Africa reflects its own priorities. These include countering Western influence, building non-aligned partnerships and advancing multilateral reform. Expanding defence sales, securing minerals access and mitigating the impact of sanctions are also priorities. 

Moscow has pursued these objectives partly by using the BRICS grouping, which includes South Africa, Egypt and Ethiopia. It has also maintained its own bilateral political, security and economic relationships.

The summit, which will be accompanied by an economic and humanitarian forum, speaks directly to Moscow’s interests while also responding to African priorities. It is expected to promote new payment systems, reform of global financial institutions, stronger African representation at international organizations and opposition to unilateral sanctions. It will also discuss trade and investment, food and energy security, nuclear energy, technology and security cooperation. 

The summit is expected to produce a joint declaration, a separate declaration on AI cooperation, and an action plan for 2027–2029.

Russia’s deepening footprint

Security has been one of Russia’s main focuses in Africa. Since 2023, Africa Corps – the Russian state-controlled paramilitary force that replaced the Wagner Group – has expanded its presence. It has deployed beyond Mali, the Central African Republic and Libya to Burkina Faso and Niger. There are also reports pointing at possible deployments in Togo, which signed a military cooperation agreement with Moscow in 2025.

As insurgent attacks persist in the Sahel, Russia has deepened its ties with the Alliance of Sahel States (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger), pledging military and technical support. The three states have increasingly turned to Russia for security and diplomatic support following their break from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), and amid deteriorating relations with Western partners. Russia is also pursuing a parallel security cooperation agreement with ECOWAS, which will cover the broader region. 

Related work

Mali attacks show security cannot be delivered by military means alone

Diplomatically, Moscow has expanded its network of embassies on the continent, with planned missions bringing the total to 49. Russia has also sought to extend its diplomatic reach to the Horn of Africa amid rising tensions there, offering to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea on the margins of the summit in Moscow. The proposal signals Moscow’s ambition to position itself as a security interlocutor beyond the Sahel, although it remains an offer rather than a confirmed mediation effort.

Russia has also sought to deepen its economic footprint in Africa. Russian agricultural exports to Africa grew 35 percent in value in the first half of 2026, to $2.9 billion, with wheat shipments reaching record volumes. 

It has signed intergovernmental nuclear cooperation agreements with at least 15 African states.  For example, Rosatom, the Russian state nuclear corporation, signed an agreement to build a nuclear power plant in Ethiopia.   

Russia is also working with the African Union. At a July 2026 consultation in Addis Ababa, both sides committed to annual high-level political consultations and to launch sectoral dialogues. 

Limited returns

However, despite Russia’s deepening involvement in sectors such as energy and agricultural exports, trade between Africa and Russia is estimated at $27 billion in 2025, well below the $40 billion target announced by Putin in 2019.  It also pales in comparison to the EU’s €355 billion ($395 billon) and China’s $348 billion of recorded trade with Africa in 2025. 

In June, Russia’s foreign ministry acknowledged at a forum in St Petersburg that previous summits had produced more declaration than deals. It promised this third summit will be different.  

Related work

Can Africa maximize its global influence?

Agreements on nuclear power are yet to translate into completed projects. Egypt’s El Dabaa plant is still under construction. Ethiopia’s nuclear power plant is still at a prospective stage. 

Even in defence, the picture is not favourable. Russian global arms exports declined by 64 percent in 2021-2025. Russia ranked third, behind the US and China, in major arms supply to Africa during the same period. 

Russia’s increased security role in the Sahel has also failed to deliver reliable security guarantees. Annual deaths linked to violent extremism in the Sahel have increased from an average of 927 in 2016–2019 to an average of 10,470 in 2022–2025. 

In April 2026, a coalition of Tuareg separatists and al-Qaeda-linked jihadists killed Mali’s defence Minister and forced Africa Corps personnel to withdraw from the northern city of Kidal. Russian-backed forces subsequently regained control of Kidal in October, but the episode has exposed the limits of their security model. 

Russian-linked actors have sought to offset the costs of the war through security-for-resources arrangements, including control of and revenue from African gold mines; the US Treasury reports that gold and other African resources have helped Russia evade sanctions and fund its military efforts in Ukraine. 

There is also the question of the extent to which Russia can sustain its security commitments in Africa while its resources and attention remain stretched by the war in Ukraine.

Recruiting for the Ukraine war

Russia’s recruitment of African citizens to fight in Ukraine has become a reputational liability. A recent investigation cited by African media outlets estimated that more than 3,000 African citizens from 40 countries were recruited into Russia’s armed forces between October 2022 and June 2026, often through deception and promises of civilian jobs. Bloomberg reported this week that Moscow has been widening its recruitment drive in countries including Zimbabwe, Burundi and Sierra Leone. 

Related work

After Trump’s Russian diesel deal, will Europe give Ukraine the support it needs? 

African countries including Kenya and South Africa have sought to stop the recruitment of their citizens. During a visit to Moscow in April, Kenya’s foreign minister Musalia Mudavadi said that Moscow and Nairobi had agreed that Kenyan nationals would no longer be enlisted by Russia’s ministry of defence. Russia’s embassy in Nairobi had denied any involvement in recruitment.

An Afrobarometer survey of citizens across 38 African countries in 2024–2025 found that the perception of Russian influence was far less positive than that of China, the US, the EU and others, and 72 per cent of those who had heard of the Ukraine war wanted their country to remain neutral in it.

From rhetoric to delivery

The pattern of African engagement with Russia is best understood as diversified non-alignment. African governments see Moscow as one of several partners with whom they can pursue their interests in trade, security and greater representation in international forums. 

With Russia’s capacity constrained by the war in Ukraine, which continues to drain resources and diplomatic bandwidth, the real test is whether Moscow can convert political declarations and security interests into concrete, deliverable commitments in other fields.

Ultimately, Russia’s standing as a partner will depend on its ability to provide sustained economic benefits, reliable security partnerships and tangible outcomes for African countries. The summit will indicate the scale of Moscow’s ambitions; the years that follow will reveal how far it can realistically meet them.

item.title: The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump | Editorial
item.description:
If ever enacted, proposals by Marine Le Pen and the AfD leader, Alice Weidel, to hollow out EU institutions would be a continental act of self-harm

Following the Brexit referendum in 2016, Marine Le Pen was in a predictably celebratory mood. Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, she told one interviewer, was the first breach in the “Brussels Wall”. Ms Le Pen’s Front National party was at that point committed to taking France down the same path, given the chance. But as the UK’s self-inflicted economic wounds became a cautionary tale for the rest of Europe, the notion of Frexit was put on ice.

Instead, Ms Le Pen now hopes to lead far-right allies in hollowing out the EU from within. This month, both she and the leader of Alternative für Deutschland, Alice Weidel, outlined their visions of a “Europe of nations” in which EU institutions would be stripped of both cash and power. Ms Weidel’s “new deal for Europe” would abolish elections to the European parliament, and seek German opt-outs in areas such as migration, defence and common borrowing. Ms Le Pen’s party, now called National Rally, proposes slashing French contributions to the EU budget by 60% over a five-year presidential term, and ending the role of Brussels in proposing common policies for the 27 member states.
